notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space.
  • Matter is composed of extremely small particles.
  • Atoms and molecules are basic particles used to describe matter.
  • Pure substances are broadly classified as elements and compounds.
  • Mixtures contain two or more substances physically combined.
  • Matter may exist as solid, liquid, gas, plasma and other specialised states.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Matter → Pure Substances + Mixtures

Pure Substances → Elements + Compounds

2. Pure Substance
  • A pure substance has a definite and uniform composition.
  • Elements are pure substances.
  • Compounds are pure substances.
  • Pure substances have characteristic physical and chemical properties.
  • Pure substances cannot be separated into components by ordinary physical separation methods.
3. Element
  • An element is a pure substance composed of only one type of atom.
  • An element cannot be broken into simpler substances by ordinary chemical reactions.
  • Each element has a unique atomic number.
  • Elements are represented by chemical symbols.
  • Examples include hydrogen, oxygen, carbon, iron and gold.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Element → One Type of Atom

4. Number of Known Elements
  • The modern periodic table contains 118 officially recognised elements.
  • Hydrogen has atomic number 1.
  • Oganesson has atomic number 118.
  • Elements are arranged primarily according to increasing atomic number.
📌 Remember

First Element → Hydrogen

Element 118 → Oganesson

5. Atom
  • An atom is the smallest unit of an element that retains its chemical identity.
  • Atoms contain a nucleus and electrons.
  • The nucleus contains protons and neutrons.
  • Electrons occupy regions around the nucleus.
  • Atoms are electrically neutral when proton and electron numbers are equal.
6. Subatomic Particles
  • Proton → Positive charge.
  • Neutron → No net charge.
  • Electron → Negative charge.
  • Proton and neutron are located in the nucleus.
  • Electrons are found outside the nucleus.
7. Atomic Number
  • Atomic number is represented by Z.
  • Atomic number equals number of protons.
  • In a neutral atom, atomic number also equals number of electrons.
  • Atomic number uniquely identifies an element.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Atomic Number → Proton Number

8. Mass Number
  • Mass number is represented by A.
  • Mass number = Protons + Neutrons.
  • A = Z + N.
  • Number of neutrons = A − Z.
  • Mass number is always a whole number for an individual nuclide.
9. Atomic Mass
  • Atomic mass is the mass of an atom relative to the atomic mass unit.
  • Relative atomic masses shown in the periodic table are generally weighted averages of naturally occurring isotopes.
  • Therefore, many listed atomic masses are not whole numbers.
  • Carbon has a relative atomic mass close to 12.01 because of isotopic abundance.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Mass number → Whole number for a particular isotope.

Relative atomic mass → Often decimal.

10. Atomic Mass Unit
  • Atomic mass unit is represented by u.
  • 1 u is defined as one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
  • 1 u ≈ 1.6605 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
  • Atomic and molecular masses are conveniently expressed in u.
11. Isotopes
  • Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
  • They have the same number of protons.
  • They differ in neutron number.
  • Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are isotopes.
  • Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 are isotopes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Isotopes → Same Z, Different A

12. Molecule
  • A molecule consists of two or more atoms chemically bonded together.
  • A molecule may contain atoms of the same element.
  • It may also contain atoms of different elements.
  • O₂ is a molecule of an element.
  • H₂O is a molecule of a compound.
13. Atomicity
  • Atomicity is the number of atoms present in one molecule of an element in basic textbook usage.
  • Monatomic substances contain one atom per particle.
  • Diatomic molecules contain two atoms.
  • Triatomic molecules contain three atoms.
  • Polyatomic molecules contain more atoms.
14. Monatomic Elements
  • Noble gases commonly exist as monatomic gases.
  • Helium → He.
  • Neon → Ne.
  • Argon → Ar.
  • Krypton → Kr.
  • Xenon → Xe.
  • Radon → Rn.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Noble Gases → Monatomic

15. Diatomic Elements

Important diatomic elements under ordinary conditions include:

  • Hydrogen → H₂.
  • Nitrogen → N₂.
  • Oxygen → O₂.
  • Fluorine → F₂.
  • Chlorine → Cl₂.
  • Bromine → Br₂.
  • Iodine → I₂.
📌 Memory

H₂ N₂ O₂ F₂ Cl₂ Br₂ I₂

16. Triatomic Molecule
  • Ozone has molecular formula O₃.
  • Ozone is an allotrope of oxygen.
  • It contains three oxygen atoms.
  • Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs much harmful ultraviolet radiation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ozone → O₃

17. Compound
  • A compound is a pure substance formed by chemical combination of two or more elements in fixed proportions.
  • Components of a compound lose their individual properties.
  • A compound has properties different from its constituent elements.
  • Compounds can be decomposed by chemical methods.
  • Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Compound → Elements Chemically Combined in Fixed Ratio

18. Water as a Compound
  • Water has formula H₂O.
  • Each water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
  • Hydrogen and oxygen are gases under ordinary conditions.
  • Water is a liquid under ordinary conditions.
  • This demonstrates that compounds can have properties very different from their constituent elements.
19. Mixture
  • A mixture contains two or more substances physically combined.
  • Components retain many of their individual properties.
  • Composition can vary.
  • Components can usually be separated by physical methods.
  • Air is a mixture of gases.
  • Salt solution is a homogeneous mixture.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mixture → Variable Composition + Physical Separation

20. Compound vs Mixture
  • Compound has fixed composition.
  • Mixture can have variable composition.
  • Compound is formed through chemical combination.
  • Mixture is formed through physical mixing.
  • Compound constituents cannot generally be separated by simple physical methods.
  • Mixture components can often be separated physically.
  • Compounds have definite chemical formulae.
  • Mixtures do not have one fixed chemical formula.
21. Homogeneous Mixture
  • A homogeneous mixture has uniform composition throughout.
  • It appears as a single phase.
  • Salt solution is homogeneous.
  • Sugar solution is homogeneous.
  • Air is generally treated as a homogeneous gaseous mixture.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Homogeneous → Uniform Composition

22. Heterogeneous Mixture
  • A heterogeneous mixture does not have uniform composition throughout.
  • Different phases or components may be distinguishable.
  • Sand and water form a heterogeneous mixture.
  • Oil and water form a heterogeneous mixture.
  • Soil is a heterogeneous mixture.
23. Solution
  • A solution is a homogeneous mixture.
  • It contains a solute and solvent.
  • Solute is the substance dissolved.
  • Solvent is the medium that dissolves the solute.
  • Salt water contains salt as solute and water as solvent.
24. Solute
  • Solute is generally present in smaller amount in a simple solution.
  • It is dissolved in the solvent.
  • A solution may contain more than one solute.
  • Salt and sugar can both act as solutes.
25. Solvent
  • Solvent dissolves the solute.
  • Water is an important solvent.
  • Water is often called a universal solvent because it dissolves many substances.
  • Water does not dissolve every substance.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Water is called a universal solvent, but it does not dissolve all substances.

26. Suspension
  • A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture.
  • Particles are relatively large.
  • Particles can settle on standing.
  • Suspension particles can often be separated by filtration.
  • Muddy water is an example.
27. Colloid
  • A colloid has particle sizes intermediate between true solutions and coarse suspensions.
  • Colloidal particles do not readily settle under gravity.
  • Colloids scatter light.
  • This scattering is called the Tyndall effect.
  • Milk is a colloidal system.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Colloid → Tyndall Effect

28. Tyndall Effect
  • Tyndall effect is scattering of light by colloidal particles.
  • It makes the path of a beam visible.
  • Fog and smoke show light scattering.
  • A true solution generally does not show a strong Tyndall effect.
29. Chemical Symbol
  • A chemical symbol is a shorthand representation of an element.
  • Symbols generally contain one or two letters.
  • First letter is always capital.
  • Second letter, if present, is lowercase.
  • Hydrogen → H.
  • Helium → He.
  • Calcium → Ca.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

CO ≠ Co

CO → Carbon monoxide

Co → Cobalt

30. Symbols Derived from Latin Names

Important examples:

  • Sodium → Na → Natrium.
  • Potassium → K → Kalium.
  • Iron → Fe → Ferrum.
  • Copper → Cu → Cuprum.
  • Silver → Ag → Argentum.
  • Gold → Au → Aurum.
  • Mercury → Hg → Hydrargyrum.
  • Lead → Pb → Plumbum.
  • Tin → Sn → Stannum.
📌 Must-Memorise

Na, K, Fe, Cu, Ag, Au, Hg, Pb, Sn

31. Chemical Formula
  • A chemical formula represents the kinds and numbers of atoms in a substance.
  • H₂O means two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
  • CO₂ means one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms.
  • NH₃ means one nitrogen and three hydrogen atoms.
  • CH₄ means one carbon and four hydrogen atoms.
32. Subscript in Formula
  • A subscript shows the number of atoms of an element in one molecule or formula unit.
  • H₂O contains two H atoms.
  • CO₂ contains two O atoms.
  • If no subscript is written, the implied number is one.
33. Coefficient in Chemical Equation
  • A coefficient indicates the number of molecules or formula units.
  • 2H₂O means two water molecules.
  • 2H₂O therefore contains four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms.
  • Coefficients are changed when balancing chemical equations.
  • Subscripts should not be changed merely to balance an equation.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Balance equations by changing coefficients, not chemical subscripts.

34. Valency
  • Valency is the combining capacity of an atom or ion.
  • It is related to electrons lost, gained or shared during bonding.
  • Hydrogen generally has valency 1.
  • Oxygen generally has valency 2.
  • Nitrogen commonly has valency 3.
  • Carbon commonly has valency 4.
📌 Must-Memorise

H → 1

O → 2

N → 3

C → 4

35. Variable Valency

Some elements show more than one common valency.

Examples:

  • Iron → 2 and 3.
  • Copper → 1 and 2.
  • Tin → 2 and 4.
  • Lead → 2 and 4.
  • Mercury → 1 and 2 in traditional valency descriptions.
36. Ion
  • An ion is an electrically charged atom or group of atoms.
  • Ions form when electrons are lost or gained.
  • Positive ions are called cations.
  • Negative ions are called anions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Cation → Positive

Anion → Negative

37. Cation
  • A cation forms when an atom loses one or more electrons.
  • Sodium ion is Na⁺.
  • Calcium ion is Ca²⁺.
  • Aluminium ion is Al³⁺.
  • Metals commonly form cations.
38. Anion
  • An anion forms when an atom gains one or more electrons.
  • Chloride ion is Cl⁻.
  • Oxide ion is O²⁻.
  • Nitride ion is N³⁻.
  • Non-metals commonly form anions.
39. Polyatomic Ions

Important polyatomic ions include:

  • Ammonium → NH₄⁺.
  • Hydroxide → OH⁻.
  • Nitrate → NO₃⁻.
  • Sulfate → SO₄²⁻.
  • Carbonate → CO₃²⁻.
  • Bicarbonate/Hydrogen carbonate → HCO₃⁻.
  • Phosphate → PO₄³⁻.
📌 Must-Memorise

NH₄⁺, OH⁻, NO₃⁻, SO₄²⁻, CO₃²⁻, HCO₃⁻, PO₄³⁻

40. Chemical Bond
  • A chemical bond holds atoms or ions together.
  • Important bond types include ionic, covalent and metallic bonding.
  • Bond formation generally leads to a lower-energy, more stable arrangement.
41. Ionic Bond
  • Ionic bonding involves electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
  • It commonly forms between a metal and non-metal.
  • Electron transfer produces ions.
  • Sodium chloride is a classic ionic compound.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ionic Bond → Electron Transfer + Opposite Ions

42. Formation of Sodium Chloride
  • Sodium has one valence electron.
  • Chlorine has seven valence electrons.
  • Sodium loses one electron to form Na⁺.
  • Chlorine gains one electron to form Cl⁻.
  • Electrostatic attraction forms sodium chloride.
📌 Formula

Na⁺ + Cl⁻ → NaCl

43. Properties of Ionic Compounds
  • Ionic compounds are generally crystalline solids.
  • They often have high melting and boiling points.
  • They are often soluble in polar solvents such as water.
  • Solid ionic compounds generally do not conduct electricity.
  • Molten ionic compounds conduct electricity.
  • Aqueous ionic solutions conduct electricity.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Solid NaCl → Poor electrical conductor.

Molten NaCl → Conducts electricity.

44. Covalent Bond
  • Covalent bonding involves sharing of electron pairs between atoms.
  • It commonly occurs between non-metals.
  • H₂, O₂, H₂O and CH₄ contain covalent bonds.
  • Covalent molecules may be non-polar or polar.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Covalent Bond → Electron Sharing

45. Single Covalent Bond
  • A single covalent bond contains one shared pair of electrons.
  • H₂ contains a single bond.
  • HCl contains a single covalent bond.
  • C–H bonds in methane are single bonds.
46. Double Bond
  • A double bond contains two shared pairs of electrons.
  • O₂ contains a double bond in basic Lewis representation.
  • Carbon dioxide contains two C=O double bonds.
47. Triple Bond
  • A triple bond contains three shared pairs of electrons.
  • N₂ contains a triple bond.
  • Triple bonds are generally stronger and shorter than corresponding single bonds.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

N₂ → Triple Bond

O₂ → Double Bond

H₂ → Single Bond

48. Metallic Bond
  • Metallic bonding involves positive metal ions surrounded by delocalised electrons.
  • Mobile electrons contribute to electrical conductivity.
  • Metallic bonding explains malleability and ductility.
  • Metals generally conduct heat and electricity well.
49. Octet Rule
  • Many atoms tend to attain eight electrons in their valence shell during chemical bonding.
  • This is called the octet rule.
  • Noble gases generally possess stable valence-shell configurations.
  • Hydrogen and helium follow a duplet-type stability instead.
  • The octet rule has several exceptions.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Octet rule is a useful model, not an absolute rule for every compound.

50. Valence Electrons
  • Valence electrons are electrons in the outermost occupied shell.
  • They strongly influence chemical properties.
  • Elements in the same main-group column generally have similar valence-electron patterns.
  • Noble gases have stable outer shells.
51. Electron Shells

Traditional shell names are:

  • K.
  • L.
  • M.
  • N.

Maximum electron capacity in shell n is given by 2n².

📌 Capacities

K → 2.

L → 8.

M → 18.

N → 32.

52. Electronic Configuration — First 20 Elements

Basic shell distribution examples:

  • H → 1.
  • He → 2.
  • Li → 2,1.
  • Be → 2,2.
  • B → 2,3.
  • C → 2,4.
  • N → 2,5.
  • O → 2,6.
  • F → 2,7.
  • Ne → 2,8.
  • Na → 2,8,1.
  • Mg → 2,8,2.
  • Al → 2,8,3.
  • Si → 2,8,4.
  • P → 2,8,5.
  • S → 2,8,6.
  • Cl → 2,8,7.
  • Ar → 2,8,8.
  • K → 2,8,8,1.
  • Ca → 2,8,8,2.
53. Chemical Equation
  • A chemical equation represents a chemical reaction using symbols and formulae.
  • Reactants are written on the left.
  • Products are written on the right.
  • An arrow indicates direction of reaction.
  • Chemical equations must obey conservation of atoms.
54. Balanced Chemical Equation
  • A balanced equation has equal numbers of each type of atom on both sides.
  • Balancing follows conservation of mass.
  • Example:
  • 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.
  • Hydrogen atoms are four on both sides.
  • Oxygen atoms are two on both sides.
55. Law of Conservation of Mass
  • Mass is neither created nor destroyed in an ordinary chemical reaction.
  • Total mass of reactants equals total mass of products in a closed system.
  • Antoine Lavoisier established the law experimentally.
  • Lavoisier is often called the father of modern chemistry.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lavoisier → Conservation of Mass

56. Antoine Lavoisier
  • Antoine Lavoisier was a French chemist.
  • He helped establish quantitative chemistry.
  • He formulated the law of conservation of mass.
  • He explained the role of oxygen in combustion.
  • He opposed the old phlogiston theory.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lavoisier → Father of Modern Chemistry

57. Law of Definite Proportions
  • A pure compound always contains the same elements combined in a fixed proportion by mass.
  • The law is associated with Joseph Proust.
  • Water always contains hydrogen and oxygen in a definite mass ratio.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Proust → Definite Proportions

58. Law of Multiple Proportions
  • When two elements form more than one compound, masses of one element combining with a fixed mass of the other are in simple whole-number ratios.
  • John Dalton formulated the law of multiple proportions.
  • Carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide are a classic example.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Dalton → Multiple Proportions

59. Dalton's Atomic Theory

Major ideas included:

  • Matter consists of atoms.
  • Atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios.
  • Chemical reactions rearrange atoms.
  • Atoms are not created or destroyed in ordinary chemical reactions.
  • Some original Dalton ideas were later modified by discoveries of isotopes and subatomic particles.
60. John Dalton
  • John Dalton proposed a scientific atomic theory in the early nineteenth century.
  • His major work A New System of Chemical Philosophy began publication in 1808.
  • Dalton also formulated the law of multiple proportions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Dalton → Atomic Theory → 1808

61. Avogadro's Hypothesis
  • Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.
  • This principle is associated with Amedeo Avogadro.
  • Avogadro proposed the idea in 1811.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Avogadro → Equal Gas Volumes → Equal Number of Molecules

62. Avogadro Constant
  • One mole contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ specified elementary entities.
  • This number is called Avogadro constant.
  • Symbol is Nₐ.
  • It may refer to atoms, molecules, ions or other specified particles.
📌 Must-Memorise

Nₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹

63. Mole
  • Mole is the SI base unit for amount of substance.
  • One mole contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ elementary entities.
  • Molar mass is expressed in g/mol or kg/mol.
  • One mole of carbon-12 atoms has a mass close to 12 g.
64. Molar Mass
  • Molar mass is mass of one mole of a substance.
  • Water has molar mass approximately 18 g/mol.
  • CO₂ has molar mass approximately 44 g/mol.
  • NaCl has molar mass approximately 58.5 g/mol.
65. Molecular Mass
  • Molecular mass is the sum of relative atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule.
  • H₂O → approximately 18 u.
  • CO₂ → approximately 44 u.
  • NH₃ → approximately 17 u.
  • CH₄ → approximately 16 u.
66. Formula Mass
  • Ionic compounds do not consist of discrete molecules in their crystal lattice.
  • Their relative mass is more accurately called formula mass.
  • NaCl formula mass is approximately 58.44 u.
  • The term molecular mass is mainly appropriate for molecular substances.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

NaCl → Formula unit, not a discrete molecule in the crystal.

67. Periodic Table
  • The periodic table arranges elements according to increasing atomic number.
  • Elements with similar properties occur in groups.
  • Horizontal rows are called periods.
  • Vertical columns are called groups.
  • The modern periodic table contains 7 periods and 18 groups.
📌 Must-Memorise

Periods → 7

Groups → 18

68. Early Periodic Classification — Döbereiner
  • Johann Wolfgang Döbereiner proposed triads.
  • Groups of three elements with similar properties were called Döbereiner's triads.
  • The atomic mass of the middle element was approximately the average of the other two in successful triads.
📌 Example

Li, Na, K

🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Döbereiner → Triads

69. Newlands' Law of Octaves
  • John Newlands arranged elements by increasing atomic mass.
  • He observed that every eighth element showed similar properties in parts of his arrangement.
  • He called this the Law of Octaves.
  • It worked mainly for lighter elements known at that time.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Newlands → Law of Octaves

70. Mendeleev's Periodic Table
  • Dmitri Mendeleev proposed a major periodic classification in 1869.
  • He arranged elements mainly by increasing atomic mass and recurring chemical properties.
  • He left gaps for undiscovered elements.
  • He predicted properties of several unknown elements accurately.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mendeleev → Periodic Table → 1869

71. Mendeleev's Predictions

Mendeleev predicted elements later identified as:

  • Gallium.
  • Scandium.
  • Germanium.
  • He used names such as eka-aluminium, eka-boron and eka-silicon for predicted elements.
📌 Must-Memorise

Eka-Aluminium → Gallium

Eka-Boron → Scandium

Eka-Silicon → Germanium

72. Modern Periodic Law
  • Physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.
  • The modern periodic law is based on atomic number rather than atomic mass.
  • Henry Moseley's work established atomic number as the proper basis.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Modern Periodic Law → Atomic Number

73. Henry Moseley
  • Henry Moseley studied characteristic X-ray spectra of elements.
  • His work established atomic number as a fundamental ordering property.
  • Modern periodic classification follows increasing atomic number.
  • Moseley's work dates to 1913.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Moseley → Atomic Number → 1913

74. Periods
  • The periodic table has seven periods.
  • Period 1 contains two elements.
  • Periods 2 and 3 contain eight elements each.
  • Periods 4 and 5 contain 18 elements each.
  • Period 6 includes lanthanides.
  • Period 7 includes actinides.
75. Groups
  • The periodic table has 18 groups.
  • Elements in the same main group often have similar chemical properties.
  • Group 1 contains alkali metals.
  • Group 2 contains alkaline earth metals.
  • Group 17 contains halogens.
  • Group 18 contains noble gases.
76. Group 1 — Alkali Metals

Important alkali metals include:

  • Lithium.
  • Sodium.
  • Potassium.
  • Rubidium.
  • Caesium.
  • Francium.
  • They have one valence electron.
  • They are highly reactive.
  • They commonly form +1 ions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Group 1 → Alkali Metals → Valency 1

77. Hydrogen and Group 1
  • Hydrogen is placed above Group 1 because it has one valence electron.
  • Hydrogen is a non-metal.
  • Its properties differ substantially from alkali metals.
  • Hydrogen has a unique position in the periodic table.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Hydrogen is not an alkali metal.

78. Group 2 — Alkaline Earth Metals

Important members include:

  • Beryllium.
  • Magnesium.
  • Calcium.
  • Strontium.
  • Barium.
  • Radium.
  • They commonly form +2 ions.
  • They have two valence electrons.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Group 2 → Alkaline Earth Metals

79. Group 17 — Halogens

Members include:

  • Fluorine.
  • Chlorine.
  • Bromine.
  • Iodine.
  • Astatine.
  • Tennessine.
  • Halogens commonly have seven valence electrons.
  • They commonly form −1 ions.
  • They are reactive non-metals in the common lighter members.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Group 17 → Halogens

80. Group 18 — Noble Gases

Members include:

  • Helium.
  • Neon.
  • Argon.
  • Krypton.
  • Xenon.
  • Radon.
  • Oganesson.
  • Noble gases have stable outer-electron configurations.
  • They are comparatively unreactive.
  • Helium has two electrons in its only occupied shell.
  • Other common noble gases have eight outer-shell electrons.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Group 18 → Noble Gases

81. Transition Elements
  • Transition elements occupy the central d-block region.
  • Many show variable oxidation states.
  • Many form coloured compounds.
  • Many act as catalysts.
  • Iron, cobalt, nickel, copper and chromium are common examples in broad textbook treatment.
82. Lanthanides
  • Lanthanides are associated with atomic numbers 57–71.
  • They are often called rare-earth elements along with some related elements.
  • They occupy part of period 6.
  • They are shown separately below the main periodic table for convenience.
83. Actinides
  • Actinides are associated with atomic numbers 89–103.
  • They occupy part of period 7.
  • All actinides are radioactive.
  • Uranium and thorium are important actinide elements.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Actinides → Radioactive

84. Metals

Common properties of metals:

  • Lustrous.
  • Malleable.
  • Ductile.
  • Good conductors of heat.
  • Good conductors of electricity.
  • Generally solid at room temperature.
  • Tend to form positive ions.
85. Malleability
  • Malleability is the ability to be hammered or rolled into thin sheets.
  • Gold is highly malleable.
  • Aluminium is malleable.
  • Metals are generally more malleable than non-metals.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Malleability → Sheets

86. Ductility
  • Ductility is the ability to be drawn into wires.
  • Copper is ductile.
  • Gold is highly ductile.
  • Ductility makes metals useful in electrical wiring.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ductility → Wires

87. Sonority
  • Sonorous materials produce a ringing sound when struck.
  • Metals are generally sonorous.
  • This property is used in bells and musical instruments.
88. Mercury
  • Mercury is a metal.
  • Its symbol is Hg.
  • Mercury is liquid at ordinary room temperature.
  • It was historically used in thermometers and barometers.
  • Mercury and many of its compounds are toxic.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Liquid Metal at Room Temperature → Mercury

89. Bromine
  • Bromine is a non-metal.
  • Symbol is Br.
  • Bromine is a reddish-brown liquid at room temperature.
  • It is a halogen.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Liquid Non-Metal at Room Temperature → Bromine

90. Non-Metals

General properties include:

  • Often poor conductors.
  • Generally brittle when solid.
  • Not malleable.
  • Not ductile.
  • May occur as solids, liquids or gases.
  • Tend to gain or share electrons.
91. Graphite Exception
  • Graphite is an allotrope of carbon.
  • Carbon is a non-metal.
  • Graphite conducts electricity.
  • It contains delocalised electrons within its layered structure.
  • Graphite is therefore an important exception to the idea that non-metals do not conduct electricity.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Conducting non-metal → Graphite

92. Iodine Exception
  • Iodine is a non-metal.
  • Solid iodine has a lustrous appearance.
  • Thus lustre is not exclusively a property of metals.

  • Metalloids show properties intermediate between metals and non-metals.

  • Many metal oxides are basic.

🔗 TNPSC Key Link

  • Many non-metal oxides are acidic.

  • Amphoteric oxides react with both acids and bases.

  • Allotropy is the existence of an element in two or more different structural forms in the same physical state.

  • Diamond consists of carbon atoms.

  • Graphite consists of layered carbon structures.

  • Fullerenes are cage-like carbon structures.

  • Sulfur exhibits different crystalline forms.

  • Aluminium symbol is Al.

128. Separation of Mixtures

Important physical methods include:

  • Filtration.
  • Sedimentation.
  • Decantation.
  • Evaporation.
  • Crystallisation.
  • Sublimation.
  • Distillation.
  • Fractional distillation.

129. Filtration
  • Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid.
  • Filter paper allows liquid to pass.
  • Solid residue remains on filter paper.
  • Sand can be separated from water by filtration.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Insoluble Solid + Liquid → Filtration

130. Sedimentation
  • Sedimentation allows heavier insoluble particles to settle under gravity.
  • Muddy water can undergo sedimentation.
  • The settled material is called sediment.
131. Decantation
  • Decantation separates the clear liquid above a settled solid.
  • It can also help separate immiscible liquid layers carefully.
  • It is often used after sedimentation.
132. Evaporation
  • Evaporation removes a volatile solvent from a solution.
  • Salt can be obtained from seawater by evaporation.
  • It is not suitable when recovery of the solvent is required.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Salt from Seawater → Evaporation

133. Crystallisation
  • Crystallisation produces pure solid crystals from a solution.
  • It can purify substances containing soluble impurities.
  • It is often preferable to complete evaporation when well-formed pure crystals are required.
134. Sublimation Separation
  • Sublimation separates a sublimable solid from a non-sublimable material.
  • Ammonium chloride, camphor, iodine or naphthalene can be separated in suitable mixtures using sublimation.
135. Simple Distillation
  • Distillation involves vaporisation followed by condensation.
  • It can separate a volatile liquid from dissolved non-volatile substances.
  • It can also separate liquids with sufficiently different boiling points.
  • Distilled water can be obtained from salt water.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Distillation → Boiling + Condensation

136. Fractional Distillation
  • Fractional distillation separates miscible liquids with closer boiling points.
  • A fractionating column allows repeated vaporisation and condensation.
  • Crude petroleum is separated into fractions using fractional distillation.
  • Liquid air can also be separated by fractional distillation after liquefaction.
137. Separating Air
  • Air is a mixture.
  • Air can be liquefied by cooling and compression.
  • Components of liquid air can be separated by fractional distillation.
  • Nitrogen and oxygen have different boiling points.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Air → Mixture → Fractional Distillation

138. Separating Funnel
  • A separating funnel separates immiscible liquids.
  • Oil and water can be separated using a separating funnel.
  • The denser liquid forms the lower layer.
  • The lower layer is drained first.
139. Centrifugation
  • Centrifugation separates components using rapid rotation.
  • Denser particles move outward more strongly.
  • It is used in laboratories.
  • Cream can be separated from milk by centrifugation.
  • Blood components can be separated by centrifugation.
140. Chromatography
  • Chromatography separates substances based on different affinities for stationary and mobile phases.
  • Paper chromatography can separate dyes.
  • It is useful for analysing mixtures.
  • Pigments in ink can be separated chromatographically.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Chromatography → Separation of Dyes/Pigments

141. Magnetic Separation
  • Magnetic separation separates magnetic material from non-magnetic material.
  • Iron filings can be separated from sand using a magnet.
  • It is used in mineral processing and recycling.
142. Alloy
  • An alloy is a mixture containing a metal and one or more other elements.

  • Bronze is traditionally an alloy mainly of copper and tin.

Bronze → Copper + Tin

  • Steel is primarily an alloy of iron and carbon.

149. Chemical Change
  • A chemical change forms one or more new substances.
  • Chemical bonds are broken or formed.
  • Examples include rusting, burning and decomposition.
  • Chemical changes are generally difficult to reverse by simple physical means.
150. Physical Change
  • A physical change does not form a new chemical substance.
  • Change of state is a physical change.
  • Melting ice is a physical change.
  • Dissolving salt in water is generally treated as a physical change because salt can be recovered by evaporation.
151. Physical vs Chemical Change
  • Melting → Physical.
  • Freezing → Physical.
  • Boiling → Physical.
  • Cutting → Physical.
  • Burning → Chemical.
  • Rusting → Chemical.
  • Digestion → Chemical.
  • Photosynthesis → Chemical.
152. Combination Reaction
  • Two or more reactants combine to form a product.
  • Example:
  • CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂.
  • Combination reactions may release heat.
153. Decomposition Reaction
  • One compound breaks into simpler substances.
  • Decomposition may be caused by heat, light or electricity.
  • CaCO₃ decomposes on heating.
  • Water can be decomposed by electrolysis.
154. Thermal Decomposition
  • Heat causes decomposition.
  • CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂.
  • This reaction is important in lime manufacture.
155. Photochemical Decomposition
  • Light causes some compounds to decompose.
  • Silver chloride darkens in sunlight.
  • Silver halide chemistry historically formed the basis of photographic films.
156. Electrolytic Decomposition
  • Electricity can decompose compounds.
  • Electrolysis of water produces hydrogen and oxygen.
  • Electrolysis of molten ionic compounds can produce elements at electrodes.
157. Displacement Reaction
  • A more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound.
  • Example:
  • Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu.
  • Zinc is more reactive than copper.

More Reactive Metal → Displaces Less Reactive Metal

158. Double Displacement Reaction
  • Ions exchange partners between two compounds.
  • Precipitation and neutralisation can be double-displacement reactions.
  • Example:
  • AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl↓ + NaNO₃.
159. Precipitate
  • A precipitate is an insoluble solid formed during a reaction in solution.
  • Silver chloride forms a white precipitate.
  • Precipitation reactions are useful in chemical analysis.

  • Oxidation traditionally means addition of oxygen or removal of hydrogen.

  • Reduction traditionally means removal of oxygen or addition of hydrogen.

162. Redox Reaction
  • Redox reaction contains oxidation and reduction simultaneously.
